title: Beans: protein, fiber, calories, and nutrition

seo.title: Beans: protein, fiber, calories, and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Cooked beans commonly provide about 120–140 calories, 8–10 g protein, and 6–9 g fiber per 100 g. Variety and cooked-versus-dry form matter.
seo.search_intent: Understand the nutrition of common cooked beans, how varieties differ, and why dry, cooked, and canned values should not be mixed.

excerpt: Black, kidney, pinto, and white beans are not nutritionally identical, but many cooked varieties cluster around 8–10 g protein and 6–9 g fiber per 100 g, with roughly 120–140 calories.
content_html:
“Beans” covers a large family rather than one standardized food. Black beans, kidney beans, pinto beans, and white beans differ in fiber, minerals, and water content. The most useful approach is therefore to use representative ranges and named examples, not one universal number.

What cooked beans typically provide

Example, per 100 g cookedCaloriesProteinFiberIron
Kidney beans~127~8.7 g~6.4 g~2.9 mg
Black beans~130~8.9 g~8–9 g~2 mg
White beans~130–140~8–10 g~6–10 gvaries

The broad pattern is consistent: a 200 g serving commonly supplies roughly 17–20 g protein plus a substantial amount of fiber.

Variety changes the number, not the basic role of the food

A difference between 8.7 and 9.5 g protein per 100 g exists, but it becomes only 1.6 g across a 200 g serving. Flavor, texture, price, digestion, and the dish you are cooking are often more useful ways to choose among varieties.

Fiber is one of the strongest reasons beans stand out

Many cooked beans provide roughly 6–9 g fiber per 100 g. A 200 g portion therefore lands around 12–18 g fiber. That is a major contrast with meat, fish, eggs, or oils, which provide 0 g fiber.

Moving abruptly from almost no beans to one or two servings a day can add roughly 12–18 g fiber at once and increase gas in some people. Raising intake gradually can be more comfortable.

They contribute iron, but absorption matters

Cooked kidney beans can provide about 2.9 mg iron per 100 g, or roughly 5.8 mg in 200 g. This is nonheme iron. Vitamin C-rich foods eaten in the same meal can improve its absorption.

Dry, cooked, and canned beans are different comparison states

Dry beans often exceed 20 g protein per 100 g because they contain little water. Once cooked, their weight rises substantially as they absorb water, bringing protein concentration down toward 8–10 g per 100 g.

Canned beans are already hydrated. Compare them with cooked beans using drained values when possible. Sodium can range from very low in no-salt-added products to several hundred milligrams per serving in salted products, so the label matters.

What about all the carbohydrate?

Cooked beans commonly contain around 20–25 g total carbohydrate per 100 g, but that figure includes fiber and starch. It is not equivalent to 20–25 g of free sugar and should not be interpreted as if all carbohydrate behaves identically.

The useful takeaway

Beans are a consistent source of plant protein and fiber, with moderate differences among varieties. The biggest comparison error is usually not choosing the “wrong” bean—it is comparing 100 g dry with 100 g cooked and treating the two values as if they describe the same amount of food.

faq.question: How much protein do cooked beans have?
faq.answer: Many common varieties provide about 8–10 g per 100 g cooked, or roughly 17–20 g in a 200 g serving.

faq.question: Which bean has the most fiber?
faq.answer: It depends on variety and database entry. Many cooked beans fall around 6–9 g fiber per 100 g.

faq.question: Are canned beans less nutritious?
faq.answer: Not inherently. They are already cooked and hydrated; sodium can vary, so drained values and the label matter.
